outline: 1942 Permutations involving Grouping, Complements, and Cases

examples.solution_text:
(a) Fix Ava and choose the other $3$ members from the remaining $8$ people.
$\begin{align*}N&={}^{8}C_{3}\\&=56\end{align*}$

(b) Exclude Ben and choose all $4$ members from the remaining $8$ people.
$\begin{align*}N&={}^{8}C_{4}\\&=70\end{align*}$

(c) Fix Ava and exclude Ben. Choose the other $3$ members from the remaining $7$ people.
$\begin{align*}N&={}^{7}C_{3}\\&=35\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A team of $4$ is chosen from $10$ players, including Mia and Noah. Exactly one of Mia and Noah must be selected. How many teams are possible?
examples.solution_text:
Choose which of Mia and Noah is selected: $2$ choices. Exclude the other and choose $3$ teammates from the remaining $8$ players.
$\begin{align*}N&=2\times{}^{8}C_{3}\\&=2\times56\\&=112\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A panel of $5$ is chosen from $7$ scientists and $5$ engineers. How many panels contain exactly $2$ engineers?
examples.solution_text:
Choose $2$ engineers from $5$ and $3$ scientists from $7$. Multiply the two selection counts.
$\begin{align*}N&={}^{5}C_{2}\times{}^{7}C_{3}\\&=10\times35\\&=350\end{align*}$

examples.question_text:
(a) A committee of $4$ is chosen from $6$ seniors and $5$ juniors. How many committees contain at most $2$ juniors?
(b) Two distinct numbers are selected from $\{1,2,3,\ldots,14\}$. How many unordered pairs have an even sum?
examples.solution_text:
(a) The mutually exclusive cases are $0$, $1$ or $2$ juniors.

No juniors:
$N_{0}={}^{5}C_{0}\times{}^{6}C_{4}=15$.

One junior:
$N_{1}={}^{5}C_{1}\times{}^{6}C_{3}=100$.

Two juniors:
$N_{2}={}^{5}C_{2}\times{}^{6}C_{2}=150$.

$\begin{align*}N&=N_{0}+N_{1}+N_{2}\\&=15+100+150\\&=265\end{align*}$

(b) There are $7$ odd and $7$ even numbers. An even sum requires two odd numbers or two even numbers.
$\begin{align*}N&={}^{7}C_{2}+{}^{7}C_{2}\\&=21+21\\&=42\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A committee of $3$ is chosen from $6$ artists and $4$ musicians. How many committees contain at least one musician?
examples.solution_text:
Subtract committees with no musicians from all committees.
$\begin{align*}N&={}^{10}C_{3}-{}^{6}C_{3}\\&=120-20\\&=100\end{align*}$

examples.question_text:
(a) In how many ways can $12$ students be divided into two unlabeled teams of $6$?
(b) In how many ways can $7$ students be divided into two unlabeled groups of sizes $2$ and $5$?
(c) In how many ways can $8$ guests be assigned to three distinct rooms holding $4$, $2$ and $2$ guests respectively?
examples.solution_text:
(a) Choose $6$ students for one team; the others form the second team. Each division is counted twice because either team could be chosen first.
$\begin{align*}N&=\frac{{}^{12}C_{6}}{2!}\\&=\frac{924}{2}\\&=462\end{align*}$

(b) Choose the smaller group. Its size identifies it, so each division is counted once.
$\begin{align*}N&={}^{7}C_{2}\\&=21\end{align*}$

(c) Choose guests for the room holding $4$, then for one specified room holding $2$. The remaining guests occupy the last room.
$\begin{align*}N&={}^{8}C_{4}\times{}^{4}C_{2}\times{}^{2}C_{2}\\&=70\times6\times1\\&=420\end{align*}$

The rooms are distinct, so do not divide by $2!$ for the two rooms with equal capacities.

Choose any $3$ of the $8$ points, then subtract triples chosen entirely from the collinear points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$.
$\begin{align*}N&={}^{8}C_{3}-{}^{4}C_{3}\\&=56-4\\&=52\end{align*}$

Only the four collinear triples fail to form triangles.

examples.question_text: Seven players are divided into two unlabeled teams of $3$ and one umpire. Ella and Finn cannot be on the same team. Either may be the umpire. How many divisions are possible?
examples.solution_text:
Choose the umpire, then divide the remaining $6$ players into two unlabeled teams.
$\begin{align*}T&={}^{7}C_{1}\times\frac{{}^{6}C_{3}}{2!}\\&=7\times10\\&=70\end{align*}$

For Ella and Finn to be teammates, choose the umpire from the other $5$ players. Choose their one teammate from the remaining $4$ players; the others form the second team.
$\begin{align*}U&={}^{5}C_{1}\times{}^{4}C_{1}\\&=5\times4\\&=20\end{align*}$

This count needs no division by $2!$: the team containing Ella and Finn is identified.
$\begin{align*}N&=T-U\\&=70-20\\&=50\end{align*}$

Choose $6$ vertices from $9$. Choose $3$ of these for one triangle; the remaining $3$ form the other.

Divide by $2!$ because exchanging the two triangles gives the same pair.
$\begin{align*}N&={}^{9}C_{6}\times\frac{{}^{6}C_{3}}{2!}\\&=84\times\frac{20}{2}\\&=840\end{align*}$

coverage.summary: Authored nine worked examples covering every distinct assessed method, including parity cases, distinct-room assignments and umpire conflicts. All 27 assessment locators are mapped individually. Questions and solutions are separate editable fields; prose uses inherited solution blue, and aligned calculations use single-dollar mathematics with relation-sign gutters. Diagrams use black ink and explicit 10 pt ordinary labels. Final-size visual verification remains for the later capture stage.

examples.derivation: Fixing Ava gives C(8,3)=56; excluding Ben gives C(8,4)=70; fixing Ava and excluding Ben gives C(7,3)=35.
The two mutually exclusive choices of specified player each allow C(8,3)=56 teams, giving 2×56=112.
Choose two engineers and three scientists: C(5,2)C(7,3)=10×35=350.
(a) Zero, one and two juniors give 15, 100 and 150 committees, totalling 265. (b) Seven odd and seven even numbers give C(7,2)+C(7,2)=42 even-sum pairs.

(a) C(12,6)/2=924/2=462 unlabeled equal-team divisions. (b) C(7,2)=21 divisions identified by the smaller group. (c) Distinct rooms give C(8,4)C(4,2)C(2,2)=70×6×1=420, without division for equal capacities.
C(8,3)−C(4,3)=56−4=52 triangles. Coordinate determinants confirm that ABC, ABD, ACD and BCD are the only collinear triples. The diagram contains exactly eight points and matches the givens.

All divisions number 7C(6,3)/2=70. Forbidden divisions number 5×4=20: choose another player as umpire and one teammate for Ella and Finn. Their team is identified, so no further division applies. Valid divisions number 70−20=50.
Choose six vertices and partition them into two unordered triples: C(9,6)C(6,3)/2=84×20/2=840. Nine distinct points at 40-degree intervals match the diagram; every triple forms a triangle.
